stories.topic: India's Founding Leaders Learned Governance as City Bosses
stories.summary: Amit points out that under the British, Indian local governments had real powers over local tasks the colonial state couldn't be bothered with. C. Rajagopalachari was effectively mayor of Salem in 1917 as chairman of the municipal board. Jawaharlal Nehru held a similar post in Allahabad in 1923. Chittaranjan Das and then Subhas Chandra Bose held it in Calcutta, and Sardar Patel was prominent in municipal politics. After independence, India kept the colonial coercive superstructure and lost this empowered local layer.
stories.insight: The freedom movement's leaders were not only activists. Running cities was their training ground in governance and public finance. Modern India dismantled the very crucible that produced its first prime minister and home minister.
stories.quote: So it is not exactly true that all of these great leaders, some of whom you know were actually a prime minister and home minister when we got independence, that they just went from being activists to politicians. It wasn't like that at all. They knew governance, they cared deeply about it, they understood public finance.

stories.topic: Uttar Pradesh Is Four European Countries
stories.summary: From his conversations with Karthik Muralidharan, Amit relays that India's 15 biggest states would each rank among the world's top 42 countries by population. By his own calculation, Uttar Pradesh is as big as France, Germany, Italy and Spain combined, all run by one state government. Karthik also notes that the average Indian district is bigger than 85 countries. Yet only 3% of India's budget is spent at the local level, against about 50% in supposedly centralised China.
stories.insight: We call these units 'states' and 'districts', but they are country-sized. Each of those 85 countries would demand its own democracy, while an Indian district gets almost no say and almost no money of its own.
stories.quote: Uttar Pradesh is the size of France, Germany, Italy and Spain combined. Right, it is that big.

stories.topic: Kerala Was Three Steps Ahead on COVID
stories.summary: Malayali students studying in China brought COVID home, so Kerala faced the first surge before almost anyone else in India. Its capable health system was already running quarantines and isolation. The Union government first did nothing and then announced nationwide lockdowns. Kerala's health authorities pushed back, saying they knew what they were doing.
stories.insight: Where a state has built real capability, instructions from New Delhi are a downgrade. Whoever holds the local knowledge should be making the decisions.
stories.quote: We know what to do. Don't tell us what to do. We are probably three steps ahead of you.

stories.topic: Susan Thomas, a Dog Bite, and a Kerala Government Clinic
stories.summary: Susan Thomas was bitten by a family dog. She insists it was her fault because she was troubling the dog. Ajay lists the surprises that followed. First, her family took her to a government clinic without a second thought, which people like them rarely do elsewhere in India. Second, the doctor was actually present and competent. Third, he asked the right questions: is it a family dog, is it healthy, will it be under observation? He then gave only antiseptic, since a rabid dog would collapse first and that would be the moment to start vaccinating. Most Indian doctors, public or private, would have 'blasted' a full course of rabies injections.
stories.insight: One-size-fits-all policy fails because state capacity itself differs hugely across India. Someone who favours radical health reform for most of the country should still respect and keep what Kerala has built.
stories.quote: I may be radical in my views on the health system, but I respect what Kerala has in a government run health system.

stories.summary: Dr Lancelot Pinto treated Amit through COVID twice. His approach was to avoid over-medication. Many deaths, he believed, came from demanding patients being overmedicated, which made their immune systems overreact. He started Amit on paracetamol and escalated step by step, and Amit never needed more than paracetamol and cough syrup.
stories.insight: Good practice can mean doing less. That takes courage, because a doctor who goes by the defensive playbook is protected from blame when random bad outcomes happen.
stories.quote: it was a structured approach and not play by the book, which is especially courageous because playing by the book is a safe thing to do.

stories.topic: The Catholic Church's Secret Sauce Was Subsidiarity
stories.summary: Economists parrot the subsidiarity principle as their own, but Ajay traces it to the Catholic Church. From around 380 to about 1950, the Church was a major world power. The Vatican controlled armies, took part in international treaties, and outlived most empires. Churches everywhere had their own autonomy, and central control was kept to the bare minimum.
stories.insight: Decentralisation is a proven design for institutions that last. Empires that centralised tended to crash, while a decentralised Church lasted more than 1,500 years.
stories.quote: Empires tended to crash partly because empires did more centralizing. And one of the design secrets of the Catholic Church was decentralization.

stories.topic: The Dutch Tanks Run by the German Army
stories.summary: After World War II the Netherlands went back to buying German tanks. As a small NATO member with perhaps twenty tanks, it found that maintaining its own logistics tail and fixed costs made no sense at that scale. So the Dutch paid for the tanks but placed them under German army command, with Dutch soldiers serving inside fully integrated German units.
stories.insight: This is the European Union's design philosophy in miniature. Instead of defining the state by lines on maps, each function goes to the scale where it works: one currency, shared defence, and local personal law.
stories.quote: We'll pay for the tanks, but the tanks will be controlled by the German army on our behalf.

stories.topic: The Monkey and the Two Cats
stories.summary: Amit retells Pranay Kotasthane's fable. Two cats fight over a piece of bread, and a monkey offers to split it fairly. Each time one half is bigger, he eats a bit of it, overshoots, and eats from the other half. When only two tiny equal crumbs remain, he takes those too as payment for his labour. Pranay uses it to show that Indian states fight over horizontal devolution (which state gets what share) while ignoring vertical devolution (how much the centre passes down at all, about 42% to states).
stories.insight: The loud debate between states, such as the South complaining it subsidises the North, distracts from the bigger issue: the centre keeps most of the bread.
stories.quote: But hey, I put in so much labor doing this, I need to be paid for my efforts

stories.topic: Nehru's Trick of Amending Away Unconstitutionality
stories.summary: Drawing on a talk by Shruti Rajagopalan, Amit explains that Nehru began the practice of amending the Constitution whenever he wanted to do something unconstitutional, so the courts couldn't stop him. It happened so often that an early cartoon showed a reader asking the parliament bookshop for a copy of the Constitution and being told the shop doesn't stock periodicals.
stories.insight: A constitution that the government of the day can rewrite at will stops restraining power and starts serving it.
stories.quote: And Nehru started this practice that every time he wanted to do something unconstitutional, he would amend the constitution and make it constitutional, which is a cunning trick and therefore the courts can't bother you.

recommendations.item: Lant Pritchett Is on Team Prosperity (Episode 379 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Lant Pritchett
recommendations.context: Amit opens the episode by mentioning his recent conversation with 'the great economist' Lant Pritchett.
recommendations.reason: While researching it, Amit arrived at the framing that sets up this episode: nation-states grew top-down and coercive, while city governments grew bottom-up and responsive. He says no amount of time could have done Pritchett justice.

recommendations.item: CMIE Consumer Pyramids dx
recommendations.creator: CMIE
recommendations.context: Ajay's go-to household survey data, which divides India into about 100 homogeneous regions of roughly seven districts each.
recommendations.reason: It makes India's heterogeneity measurable. Average income differs about 5x between the richest and poorest regions, and young women's mobile phone ownership differs 10-15x.

recommendations.item: From Imperial to Adaptive Firms (Episode 37 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay points back to this earlier episode while discussing heterogeneity.
recommendations.reason: It applies the same intuition to business. One firm design can cover a homogeneous country like Germany, but firms in India must build in the information and incentives to cope with its diversity.

recommendations.item: Metrics of Empowerment (Episode 88 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Devika Kher, Nidhi Gupta and Hamsini Hariharan
recommendations.context: Amit brings it up after Ajay's metric of women owning mobile phones.
recommendations.reason: Three 'phenomenal thinkers' propose unconventional measures of women's empowerment, such as who orders the groceries in a household.

recommendations.item: We Should Celebrate Rising Divorce Rates
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's controversial column from over a decade ago, cited as his own favourite empowerment metric.
recommendations.reason: Where others bemoan rising divorce as 'becoming like the West', Amit argues it shows more women have the agency and independence to walk away from bad marriages.

recommendations.item: South vs North
recommendations.creator: Nilakantan RS
recommendations.context: Amit's source for the state-level disparity figures.
recommendations.reason: It supplies striking comparisons: life expectancy of 75 in Kerala versus 64 in UP, and infant mortality of 7 in Kerala versus 48 in Madhya Pradesh. It also shows that Kerala battles diabetes and obesity while the heartland battles malnutrition and stunting.

recommendations.item: South India Would Like to Have a Word (Episode 320 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Nilakantan RS
recommendations.context: Amit's episode with Nilakantan RS, mentioned alongside the book.
recommendations.reason: The long-form conversation behind the North-South disparities discussed in this episode.

recommendations.item: Accelerating India's Development
recommendations.creator: Karthik Muralidharan
recommendations.context: Karthik's book, 'just out', cited for data on the scale of Indian states and districts.
recommendations.reason: Source of the facts that the average district is bigger than 85 countries and that only 3% of India's budget is spent locally, against 50% in China.

recommendations.item: Karthik Muralidharan Examines the Indian State (Episode 290) and Karthik Muralidharan and the Bureaucrat's Burden (Episode 375) of The Seen and the Unseen
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Karthik Muralidharan
recommendations.context: Amit draws on his series of recorded conversations with 'our mutual friend' Karthik.
recommendations.reason: These are where Amit first learned that India's 15 biggest states would each rank among the world's top 42 countries by population, and where they discuss India's tiny local-level spending.

recommendations.item: The Practice of Medicine (Episode 229 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Lancelot Pinto
recommendations.context: An aside prompted by Ajay's story of the sensible Kerala doctor.
recommendations.reason: Pinto, 'one of the great doctors in this country', explains his don't-overmedicate approach, the same one that saw Amit through COVID twice on paracetamol and cough syrup.

recommendations.item: Brave New World
recommendations.creator: Vasant Dhar
recommendations.context: Amit plugs the show he produces before retelling Vasant's joke about Bubba.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a great podcast and asks listeners to check it out.

recommendations.item: The Fable of the Monkey and the Two Cats
recommendations.creator: Pranay Kotasthane
recommendations.context: Amit retells it while asking how money flows between India's levels of government.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a 'great newsletter post'. It shows why the vertical question (how much the centre passes down) matters more than states squabbling over their shares.

recommendations.item: Centrally Sponsored Government Schemes (Episode 17 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Pranay Kotasthane
recommendations.context: Mentioned when Ajay argues that centrally sponsored schemes should be scrapped.
recommendations.reason: Pranay made the same argument about seven years earlier: these schemes are a backdoor for central control over state subjects.

recommendations.item: Shruti Rajagopalan on India's many constitutional amendments
recommendations.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan
recommendations.context: Amit calls it a 'must watch talk' after Ajay mentions amending the Constitution.
recommendations.reason: It traces how the Constitution has been amended from Nehru onwards, including his habit of amending it whenever he wanted to do something unconstitutional.

recommendations.item: Urban Governance in India (Episode 31 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan
recommendations.context: A short, older episode Amit links for its diagnosis of Indian cities.
recommendations.reason: Shruti explains why city governance is bad: power and accountability are not linked.

recommendations.item: Exit, Voice, and Loyalty
recommendations.creator: Albert O Hirschman
recommendations.context: Ajay cites 'the great Hirschman book' when explaining migration's role in American federalism.
recommendations.reason: Its framework shows what India underuses. Indians rely on loyalty or a little voice, while Americans use exit: if you dislike your city or state, you move.

recommendations.item: Seeing Like a State
recommendations.creator: James C Scott
recommendations.context: Ajay links Scott's ideas on the state to his case for celebrating migration.
recommendations.reason: Scott's insight that early states competed for people rather than land. Bad governments lose their people, so migration works as a verdict on governance.

recommendations.item: Our Population Is Our Greatest Asset (Episode 20 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay recalls ending that episode on India's demographic transition.
recommendations.reason: Some Indian states already have China-like low birth rates, and migration from other parts of India is what offsets their demographic decline.

recommendations.item: The Power Broker
recommendations.creator: Robert Caro
recommendations.context: One of the books Amit says he'd naturally recommend on this topic but has recommended before.
recommendations.reason: Its central figure, Robert Moses, embodied the top-down planning philosophy that Jane Jacobs fought.

recommendations.item: Triumph of the City
recommendations.creator: Edward Glaeser
recommendations.context: Named with The Power Broker as a natural, previously recommended pick for a cities episode.
recommendations.reason: A book Amit would recommend on cities; he names it rather than re-pitching it in detail.

recommendations.item: The Death and Life of Great American Cities
recommendations.creator: Jane Jacobs
recommendations.context: Amit's main recommendation of the episode.
recommendations.reason: He calls it 'an absolute masterpiece'. Jacobs argued that cities grow bottom-up and are people more than buildings and highways, and Amit counts her among the great thinkers of the 20th century. Everyone who lives in a city has skin in the game.

recommendations.item: Bimal Patel's forthcoming book
recommendations.creator: Bimal Patel
recommendations.context: Ajay's recommendation, revealed as a 'great secret' because the book isn't out yet.
recommendations.reason: Patel is India's pre-eminent urban thinker and understands town planning like almost nobody else in India. Ajay says to run, not walk, when it comes out, and Amit calls him one of the great thinkers of modern India.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay cites his book with Kelkar when discussing the concentration of power.
recommendations.reason: It argues that economic growth comes from dispersing power and building a genuine republic, and that India's failures stem from an overbearing, concentrated state.

core_ideas.concept: Nation-States Grew Top-Down, Cities Grew Bottom-Up
core_ideas.explanation: Nation-states arose coercively. Their first needs were taxes and conscripts for war, with little owed in return. City governments arose organically: once enough people lived together, they needed order, rule of law and basic services, which made them responsive and nimble by nature. India inherited only the coercive nation-state structure and never let responsive government grow from below. This reframes federalism as a matter of where governments come from, not just how power is handed down.
core_ideas.quote: what we have kind of landed up in India with is essentially just the larger coercive superstructure of the nation state with no concept of what a truly responsive government is.

core_ideas.concept: Heterogeneity Is a First-Order Policy Problem
core_ideas.explanation: India's internal gaps are continental in scale. Lant Pritchett told Ajay that India's richest-to-poorest ratio resembles that of Latin America's richest place versus Africa's poorest. CMIE regions differ 5x in income and 10-15x in young women's phone ownership. Kerala has a life expectancy of 75, like Argentina, while UP's is 64, like Liberia. Kerala's infant mortality is 7 (the USA's is 6), while Madhya Pradesh's is 48. Every question about policy and the state has to start from this diversity.
core_ideas.quote: India is that diverse and that heterogeneous. And it really becomes a first order issue to think about on all questions about policy and state and actually everything.

core_ideas.concept: Both the 'What' and the 'How' of Government Vary by Place
core_ideas.explanation: Heterogeneity changes two things. First, what problems the state should tackle: air quality in North India, Arabian Sea cyclones eating Kerala's coastline, diabetes and obesity in Kerala, malnutrition and stunting in the heartland. Second, how it should tackle them, through local technologies, organisation designs and management. A single central policy sends the wrong prescription to half the country.
core_ideas.quote: people in Kerala are like WTF, this is not our problem.

core_ideas.concept: Uniform Civil Service Pay Is a Distortion
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay calls it a 'mad idea' that civil servants across India are paid essentially the same. Pay should reflect local conditions, so a civil servant in Bombay should earn more than one in Calcutta. Flattening pay means officials in rich regions are underpaid and those in poor regions overpaid, which distorts the whole design of the state.
core_ideas.quote: So in the rich parts of India the civil servants are paid a little too little and in the poor parts of India the civil servants are paid too much and that just generates so much distortion.

core_ideas.concept: Mosquitoes Can Be Controlled, but Only Locally
core_ideas.explanation: Indians have fatalistically accepted malaria, but deliberate public health action can control mosquitoes. Mosquito populations change every 100-200 km because natural selection adapts them to local weather and to the behaviour of the people they bite. So control programmes must be designed neighbourhood by neighbourhood, by local governments. Some places, such as Ladakh, may not need one at all.
core_ideas.quote: it comes as a surprise to most people in India that actually mosquitoes can be controlled and purposive state action can actually make a huge difference to mosquito control.

core_ideas.explanation: Place every government function at the lowest level that can handle it. Currency belongs at the top, because changing money at the Maharashtra-Gujarat border would be absurd. Mosquito control belongs at the village or city level. Start at the bottom, move up only when that fails, and centralise only where decentralisation is truly infeasible.
core_ideas.quote: every function of government should be placed at the lowest level at which it can be done.

core_ideas.concept: Federalism Decided Question by Question, Not by Map
core_ideas.explanation: The European Union is deliberately not a country. It pools what makes sense to pool: the euro through the European Central Bank, defence through NATO, and small armies merged into larger ones. It leaves the rest local, such as personal law that reflects Catholic thinking in Portugal and Spain and more secular norms in Northern Europe. The right scale is chosen separately for each function.
core_ideas.quote: don't draw lines on maps and then start defining the state by lines on maps.

core_ideas.concept: The Concurrent List Is a Fantasy
core_ideas.explanation: The Constitution's framers imagined the concurrent list as a space where a wise chief minister and Nehru would work things out together. The fine print says that once the Union legislates on a concurrent subject, it wins, so in practice the list belongs to the Union. Planners then went after the state list too, through centrally sponsored schemes: 'run education my way and I'll pay 65%'. That hijacks the state's 35% and imposes a central design on it. Ajay notes that much of the Constitution's federal structure echoes the Government of India Act of 1935.
core_ideas.quote: I think there should be no centrally sponsored schemes. And I think the union should vacate the concurrent list. Okay, that is the path to genuine decentralization.

core_ideas.concept: Cities and Villages Are Different Problems
core_ideas.explanation: The 73rd and 74th Amendments, pushed under Rajiv Gandhi with Mani Shankar Aiyar as a key thinker, treated village and city government as twin projects. A village of about 150 households, or 600 people, lacks the economies of scale for enough civil servants, politicians, competition, and checks and balances. Research finds only weak gains from village-level decentralisation. Cities, some bigger than whole countries (greater Bombay outnumbers Australia), clearly have the scale to run serious governments.
core_ideas.quote: So I'm not a romantic about village level government.

core_ideas.explanation: Unlike income tax, GST can be traced to where each transaction happens, the shop, and so to a city. The blueprint drawn up in 2003 by Vijay Kelkar, Arvind Modi and Ajay for the FRBM implementation task force imagined cities as a level of government. Ajay proposes a single-rate GST of about 10%, split roughly 3% to the Union, 2% to the state and 5% to the city. Today cities depend on two finance commissions for their money. State finance commissions are often never constituted, lack data and are not neutral, and property tax can only raise so much. A direct GST share would end this dependence.
core_ideas.quote: we should think of numbers like three, two, five, that a union needs about three, the state does not have too much work, it needs about two, and the city needs about five

core_ideas.concept: Migration Is Exit, and It Should Be Celebrated
core_ideas.explanation: In American federalism, unhappy citizens move, which is Hirschman's 'exit'. People sort themselves into places that match their values, and governments that drive people away lose their tax base. James C. Scott's insight is that early states competed for people, not land. Ajay calls the lament for migrants who left village 'paradise' for city slums a luxury belief. People choose, and urban slums usually beat villages. Migration also offsets falling birth rates in prosperous states. Amit's caveat is that Indian states feel this pressure only weakly, because most tax money flows to the centre.
core_ideas.quote: And ultimately what matters is people, not territory.

core_ideas.concept: Power and Accountability Are Unlinked in Indian Cities
core_ideas.explanation: From Shruti Rajagopalan: city residents can vote for municipal officials who have little real power. The state-level politicians who do hold power have their vote banks elsewhere, so they don't answer to city residents. City governance stays bad because of this structural mismatch.
core_ideas.quote: your governance is going to be bad because power and accountability are not linked.

core_ideas.concept: A Choice Between Bad and Bad
core_ideas.explanation: Decentralisation enthusiasts can forget that Indian chief ministers act almost like dictators. Legislatures provide little check, there is nothing like the Rajya Sabha at the state level to force negotiation, and state judiciaries are often cowed. Centralised power produces distant officials who don't know the city, while local power is held in too few hands. Advocates of decentralisation must also push for political reform at the state and city level, and Amit adds that this means reasoning from first principles rather than chanting slogans.
core_ideas.quote: my concern is that a chief minister in India is a little bit of a dictator.

core_ideas.explanation: The thesis of In Service of the Republic is that development is about dispersing power. That means co-equal executive, legislative and judicial branches that check each other. India's poverty and weak growth trace back to concentrated power and an overbearing Union. The same logic applies further down: states and cities also need to become genuine republics, not personal fiefdoms.
core_ideas.quote: If you get the checks and balances, if you get a sensible republic, then the economic growth will inevitably follow.

core_ideas.concept: A Hundred States, Many of Them Cities
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay notes that very little is best done at the state level; most of the important work happens in cities. His thumb rule is that India should have about a hundred states, with big cities as states of their own. West Bengal, for example, could be two or three states, one of them Calcutta. A city-state would deal with the Finance Commission directly and could get both a GST slice and direct transfers. This works within the existing constitutional scheme and avoids risky amendments at a time when drafting skill is poor.
core_ideas.quote: my thumb rule for India is we should be a hundred states. Okay, and many of the states should be cities and that would really improve a lot of things.

core_ideas.concept: Every Government Needs Its Own Intellectual Community
core_ideas.explanation: Decentralising power without decentralising knowledge reduces government to a raw power game. Each state and city needs its own data, researchers, public debate and critics. Janaagraha argues that India's cities fall into about 63 groups of similar cities (Bombay, New Bombay and Thane being one), and each group could share data, research and municipal services.
core_ideas.quote: Every state requires a commensurate intellectual community. You need the data sets, the thinkers, the research papers, the public debate, the criticism. Without that no government ever works well.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay opens the show with a riff on Julius Caesar's 'lean and hungry look': "Your Amit has a hungry look. Such men are dangerous. Amit, what dangerous ideas do you have to offer us?"

After Ajay's mosquito obsession and his line about there perhaps being no mosquitoes in Ladakh, Amit says: "Mosquitoes and Ladakh would be an incredible title for a rock album, a heavy metal album in fact."

The tank running gag. When Ajay says he can't resist bringing something up, Amit groans, "You can never resist talking about tanks. Fine, Ajay Shah, one more time let's talk about tanks." He then pictures a thumbnail of Ajay peering out of a tank and signs off the episode with "Ajay in a tank."

Ajay voices the Dutch attitude to Germany after WWII: "Okay, fine, we forgive you, you know, we know you invaded us a couple of times, but we let it go", and then they went back to buying German tanks.

Amit retells a joke from Vasant Dhar. Vasant's friend Bubba claims to know everyone. At Trump Tower the secretary says Donald will be so happy to see him. At the White House, Biden spots him, rushes out, and falls over a couple of times on the way. At the Vatican, Vasant loses Bubba in the crowd, and then the Pope appears on the balcony with Bubba beside him. The man next to Vasant taps him and asks: "Excuse me, who's that guy with Bubba?"
Amit on the awkward middle tier of government: "When T20 cricket became popular, people said Test cricket rahega, T20 rahega, we don't need ODIs anymore. So I think states are kinda like ODIs."

Amit: the population of Iceland equals that of Mumbai's Versova. Ajay: about 300,000, "and half of them are fishermen." Amit: "Iceland or Versova?" Ajay: "Iceland." Amit: "But yeah, we have fishermen too and we are proud of them."
As animals pile up in the episode, Ajay says, "In this episode we've got a dog, a cat, a monkey." Amit adds: "And tanks, many, many tanks."

Amit, deadpan, after Ajay held up his phone while saying 'mobile phone': "I must thank you from the bottom of my heart for assuming that I am as stupid as I am... now I know and I feel so good that I have gained new knowledge today and I know what a mobile phone looks like."

Ajay on how much of India's Constitution was carried over from colonial law: "It is remarkable how much plagiarism test would pick up things in the constitution of India that come from the Government of India Act."
Amit says there are two Ajay Shahs: a sober, analytical man of history, and "a heretic who thinks mad ideas and all of those mad ideas make sense." He demands that the heretic present himself.

A bee keeps circling Amit's head: "It seems to have fallen in love with me, and while my charms are undoubted, I would not welcome this particular attention." Ajay links it to the song lyric behind the title of the show's first episode, and Amit supplies the line: "Dragonflies are busy buzzing me."
When Ajay proposes splitting West Bengal into two or three states, one of them Calcutta, Amit offers: "I have names for the three states. Calcutta, West and Bengal."
Amit on Ajay's odd verb choices: "I love the way you combine unexpected verbs and nouns, like in a previous episode you said solving a mountain. And over here you're like building a book."

Amit quotes B.R. Ambedkar's famous verdict, "What is a village but a sink of localism, a den of ignorance and narrow mindedness". He calls it Ambedkar's argument for centralising power, given caste and the treatment of women in villages. It raises the real puzzle of how far local government should go.
